title: The Paradox of Value-Added Measures in Schools
author: Nicola Peacock
summary: Nicola Peacock examines the persistent paradox of value-added measures (VAMs) in education: they were designed to give schools credit for what they actually do rather than for the demographic advantages they inherit, but the more they are used for accountability purposes the more they produce distortions that undermine the very thing they were meant to measure. The article traces how VAMs work — controlling for prior attainment and demographic factors to isolate the school's contribution to student progress — and why this seems like obviously better than raw outcome comparisons. The paradox is that high-stakes use of VAMs systematically produces gaming: schools learn to depress baseline scores, select students at predicted inflection points, and avoid the most complex learners whose trajectories are hardest to predict. The measures designed to reward authentic educational contribution end up rewarding strategic manipulation of the measurement conditions. Peacock's analysis draws on both UK and US accountability systems and is careful to distinguish between VAMs as a research tool (genuinely useful) and VAMs as a high-stakes accountability instrument (systematically distorting). The article closes with a case for using VAMs alongside multiple qualitative indicators rather than as a primary accountability lever — preserving their diagnostic value without triggering the gaming that high stakes inevitably produce.
points: The core paradox is elegant and damaging: value-added measures were designed to give schools credit for their genuine contribution regardless of intake demographics — but the moment they become high-stakes accountability tools, schools learn to manage the measures rather than manage the learning.

The specific gaming mechanisms VAMs produce are well-documented: depressing baseline assessments to manufacture apparent progress, selecting students at predicted inflection points where score gains are most achievable, and avoiding the most complex learners whose trajectories are hardest to predict.

VAMs as a research tool and VAMs as an accountability instrument are genuinely different things: in research contexts, averaged across many schools and years, VAMs provide useful signal; as a primary accountability lever for individual schools, they produce systematic distortion of the very behavior they were meant to evaluate.

Raw outcome comparisons tell us almost nothing about school quality: comparing GCSE or exam results across schools with different intake demographics measures the prior advantages students bring rather than what the school contributed — which is why the desire for VAMs was genuine and the problem they tried to solve was real.

The practical implication for school accountability design is to use VAMs alongside qualitative indicators, inspection evidence, and longitudinal data rather than as a primary accountability lever: their diagnostic value is real when they inform rather than determine consequences, and disappears when consequences are attached.
quotes: One of the enduring challenges in education is deciding how we know whether a school has made a difference. Schools admit students with different levels of prior attainment, different experiences, different opportunities and different challenges.

For schools educating comprehensive or genuinely mixed-ability cohorts, this matters enormously. It offers a way of demonstrating impact that is fairer than raw attainment alone, and for that reason it has become one of the most influential measures of school effectiveness in many educational contexts.

What strikes me now, however, is not what the diagram includes. By separating these influences into distinct contributors, I implicitly suggested that they could be considered independently of one another.
Over the years, I have occasionally found that talking about context is interpreted as making excuses. High expectations and developmental understanding are not competing philosophies.

Neural pathways that are used repeatedly become increasingly efficient through myelination, whilst others are pruned away. Executive functions continue to mature, emotional and social experiences become increasingly salient and questions of identity, autonomy and belonging assume growing importance.

Increasingly, I find myself viewing them as emerging from an ecosystem. Teaching, relationships, family, identity, curriculum, belonging, opportunity, adversity and development do not operate independently.
Perhaps that is why I find myself returning to the diagram I drew over a year ago. Not because I think it was wrong, but because I now think it was incomplete.
